Federal judge orders Trump to restore White House access to CNN, MS Now, Politico journalists

The judge rejected the government's assertion that the ban was motivated by national security concerns.

Reuters

24 September, 2026 01:41 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File Photo | The CNN booth at the White House after US President Donald Trump announced he would ban CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House in Washington, D.C., US, September 18, 2026. REUTERS/Evan Vucci/File Photo

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

A federal judge ordered US President Donald Trump on Thursday to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico, saying his ban on the three media outlets was likely unconstitutional.

In a major setback for Trump in one of his biggest battles with the media, US District Judge Tim Kelly issued his order in a lawsuit that the news organizations filed contesting the ban that the Republican president announced on September 18.

Kelly ordered the Trump administration to immediately return the outlets’ press passes and blocked officials from enforcing the ban for 14 days. The judge rejected the government’s assertion that the ban was motivated by national security concerns.

Show Full Article

“The record lacks factual support for defendants’ contention that the revocation of plaintiffs’ hard passes will in fact protect national security or that national security will be endangered if the court orders their passes reinstated while this litigation proceeds,” he said, adding that Trump himself had stated the ban was due to “alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity” of the outlets’ reporting.

The White House and representatives for the outlets did not immeidately respond to requests for comment.

Trump had said on social media that the three outlets “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES,” and Justice Department lawyers had sought to justify the ban on national security grounds.

The three outlets sued Trump and other members of his administration in federal court in Washington on Monday, saying the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press, as well as their due process rights. They requested a temporary restraining order that would immediately reinstate their White House access while their legal challenge plays out.

The legal battle has unfolded just weeks before the November 3 midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress. Trump’s job approval ratings are at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as the Iran war and inflation.

Kelly said at a Wednesday hearing that two precedents from the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit made clear that journalists are entitled to due process before their White House press passes can be revoked. The judge added that it did not appear that the White House had given the targeted news outlets a meaningful opportunity to contest the revocation of their access.

A lawyer for the news outlets told Kelly that they were ban ned without legally required advance notice or opportunity to contest the decisions, which he said were unprecedented, unreasonable and severe punishments.

A Justice Department lawyer told the judge the Trump administration provided a sufficient explanation for the revocation of the press passes in letters sent to the news outlets on Tuesday. But the judge signaled skepticism of that argument, noting that the letters were sent after the revocation occurred and the lawsuit was filed.

In a legal filing on Tuesday, the Justice Department argued that access to the White House is a privilege, not an entitlement, and that the president has the authority to suspend access by news organizations.

A coalition of press freedom groups and dozens of news organizations filed a legal brief on Wednesday supporting the three news outlets. They asserted that “stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence.”

The brief was signed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press, Reuters, the Washington Post and Fox News, among others.

(Reporting by Jan Wolfe and Jack Queen; Additional reporting by Helen Coster, Steve Holland and Rishabh Jaiswal; Editing by Lincoln Feast.)

Dictators, and why we can’t help forgiving them: Ruth Pollard

From Myanmar to Afghanistan, Belarus to Venezuela hostile regimes that were once shunned are now quietly being normalized, writes Ruth Pollard.

Ruth Pollard

24 September, 2026 11:56 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

File Photo | Taliban foreign minister Amir Khan Muttaqi during a roundtable discussion at FICCI in New Delhi | ThePrint/Suraj Singh Bisht

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

You may have missed it, but hostile regimes that were once shunned are now quietly being normalized. From Myanmar to Afghanistan, Belarus to Venezuela, military dictatorships, hardline Islamists and autocrats are edging their way back into the global order.

For some, that makes perfect sense. Governments naturally prioritize security and national interest, sanctions can be hit and miss, and businesses will pursue opportunities regardless of the optics. Yet there should be a cost for regaining a seat at the table.

Take the Taliban. Five years after it seized Kabul following the chaotic US military withdrawal, it has won a series of key diplomatic gains. Taliban-appointed diplomats now control missions across a growing number of countries including China and the United Arab Emirates, and it has signed economic and security agreements with neighbors. Has this recognition come at a cost? Not at all. The regime’s repressive nature, its ties with al-Qaeda and transnational terrorism, and its crushing treatment of women and girls all continue unabated.

Show Full Article

Aaron Zelin, a fellow at the Washington Institute for Near East Policy, calls it an “accreditation cascade” — through Gulf states, Turkey and Central Asia — where governments have accepted Taliban outreach without formally recognizing its rule. He notes in his analysis of five years of Taliban diplomacy that what began as meetings with a handful of nations has developed into joint commissions, trade councils and foreign missions. The regime is now making overtures to Washington on critical minerals.

On the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week, High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk attended a meeting that implored the world to ensure that international engagement on Afghanistan was human-rights based and principled. The  governments that are cutting deals with Taliban representatives are doing anything but.

This doesn’t mean that isolating hostile regimes until they reform is the best way forward. The US has been negotiating with Belarus and easing sanctions in exchange for the release of political prisoners, while the UK is upgrading its diplomatic ties with Venezuela to support a democratic transition. And there are ways to engage without legitimizing states, or formally recognizing their governments. Representatives talk over technical and practical matters such as border movements and assistance during natural disasters. Germany, for example, explicitly says that while the Taliban hold “de facto power” it doesn’t recognize them as the legitimate government.

Nations in Asia should follow suit, particularly when it comes to dealing with Myanmar. It’s understandable that images of coup leader Min Aung Hlaing receiving an official welcome in regional capitals would cause despair among citizens, not to mention the National Unity Government that was formed by ousted lawmakers and other anti-junta figures.

Since the February 2021 coup, more than 100,000 people have been killed and 5.2 million displaced as fighting between the army and an array of ethnic militias and anti-junta groups tore the nation apart. Despite controlling as little as a quarter of the country, the military held widely condemned elections in December and January and started calling itself a government. Min Aung Hlaing was named president in April and soon embarked on a multi-nation diplomatic mission to China, Russia, Belarus, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia in a quest for legitimacy.

India was his first port of call. The countries share a 1,643-kilometer (1,021-mile) border, and New Delhi has every reason to communicate on issues from illegal weapons trade, drug trafficking and refugee movement. Yet it has gone far beyond that. Unlike the US and Europe, it has maintained ongoing diplomatic, military and economic contacts with the junta. On his three-day visit, Min Aung Hlaing and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi discussed critical minerals, trade and healthcare. It’s not clear whether Modi raised concerns about the discredited elections or the detention of Aung San Suu Kyi.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nation’s approach is no better. Asean is pushing a five-point consensus that aims to end the political and humanitarian crisis, while some member states are pursuing bilateral relations. It’s another clear lesson of what not to do. After denying the junta a seat at high-level meetings since 2021, Asean recently began testing that exclusion. To a chorus of criticism, foreign ministers held an informal meeting with their Myanmar counterpart in Bangkok in July.

Still, perhaps the gathering managed to extract a small price. The regime has since released photographs of Suu Kyi meeting an International Committee of the Red Cross representative, although it continues to reject Asean’s calls for her unconditional release and hasn’t allowed it access to her.

University of Stirling senior international politics lecturer Monalisa Adhikari has reviewed Myanmar’s outreach since the coup, tracking how the military-backed government projected normalcy through dealings with other states. She told me that nations should be clear about whether diplomatic actions constitute formal recognition or are simply technical contacts on practical issues. That would prevent the regime from portraying such engagement as an acknowledgement of its legitimacy.

When hostile regimes are allowed to reintegrate into the global order without reducing any of their abuses, it can undercut the leverage used to  resolve conflicts and strengthen their hold on power. Engagement isn’t the problem. Normalization without conditions is. If refusing every demand for change carries no lasting cost because relations are eventually restored anyway, why would anyone comply?

Ruth Pollard is a Bloomberg Opinion Managing Editor. Previously she was South and Southeast Asia government team leader at Bloomberg News and Middle East correspondent for the Sydney Morning Herald.

Pakistan says it launched air strikes on Afghanistan in response to drone attacks

The strikes come as tensions escalate between the allies-turned-foes, who have long been at odds over attacks by Islamist militants.

Reuters

24 September, 2026 11:35 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

Representational Image | A man retrieves belongings from the debris of a house that was damaged in what the Taliban said was a Pakistani airstrike in Kunar province, Afghanistan, September 21, 2026. REUTERS/Stringer

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

Pakistan conducted airstrikes on 10 locations in Afghanistan that it said were being used to launch and store drones, some of which had been used against Pakistan a day earlier, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said on Thursday.

The strikes come as tensions escalate between the allies-turned-foes, who have long been at odds over attacks by Islamist militants, which also triggered their worst fighting in years in February.

Islamabad accuses Kabul of harbouring militants who stage cross-border attacks, but Afghanistan’s Taliban government denies harbouring anti- Pakistan i insurgents and says militancy is Pakistan ‘s internal problem.

Show Full Article

Pakistan ‘s air defence systems detected drones launched from Afghan territory on Wednesday, which were tracked and neutralised before they could reach any of their intended targets, Tarar said in a post on X.

Pakistan then conducted the “precision aerial and drone strikes” on 10 locations, which were “limited to identified military objectives” linked to the attempted attacks, he said.

“Any further provocative act by Afghan Taliban will be responded with firm and resolute response,” the minister said.

The Pakistan i airstrikes were conducted in several areas of the southeastern Khost province, Mustaghfir Gurbaz, spokesperson for the Khost governor, said.

There were no casualties, he said.

An attack on a police facility in northwestern Pakistan last week, which killed at least 24 people, has reignited fighting between the countries after nearly three months of relative calm.

Pakistan ‘s government earlier this week also said it had launched airstrikes in the Afghanistan- Pakistan border region, killing 28 militants, while Afghan Taliban officials accused Islamabad of killing three civilians in overnight strikes on Afghan territory.

The worst single incident, however, occurred in March, when more than 400 people were killed in a Pakistan i airstrike on Kabul, which the Afghan Taliban said hit a drug rehabilitation centre.

Islamabad denied the charge, saying it “precisely targeted military installations and terrorist support infrastructure”.

(Reporting by Carlos Méndez in Mexico City and Sayed Hassib in Kabul; Writing by Sakshi Dayal; Editing by Clarence Fernandez and Lincoln Feast.)

Kremlin signals before Lavrov-Rubio meeting that its stance on Ukraine peace talks remains unchanged

Reuters

23 September, 2026 04:30 pm IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

(c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

MOSCOW, Sept 23 (Reuters) – The Kremlin said on Wednesday ahead of a planned meeting in New York between US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that there were still no grounds for Ukraine peace talks to take place even though it remained open to such talks.

“For now, there are no prerequisites for moving onto a peaceful negotiating track, although we, as the Russian side, remain open to peace talks,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said he was ready to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin at a trilateral meeting with Trump, expressing hope that the US would bring Moscow to the negotiating table after talks to end the nearly five-year war unravelled earlier this year.

Show Full Article

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin stood ready to meet Trump one-on-one if both leaders deemed such a meeting necessary.

But he made it clear that Russia’s stance on the possibility of Putin and Zelenskiy meeting in person had not changed. The Kremlin has said that Zelenskiy would need to come to Moscow for such a meeting having already taken decisions Russia has been pushing for, an idea that Kyiv has repeatedly dismissed as unacceptable suggesting any talks could only be held in a neutral country.

Peskov also played down the idea of a summit: “Generally speaking, in any other circumstances, it would be inappropriate to hold a summit meeting before the groundwork has been laid at expert level, as this would be a waste of time,” he said.

(Reporting by Dmitry AntonovWriting by Alessandra Prentice Editing by Andrew Osborn )
